Cauron and his team of production designers have created what is, perhaps, the most believable vision of the future seen in quite some time. Advanced technology exists side by side with squalor, and is never allowed to steal the audience's attention away from the proceedings for too long. As far as being a realistic portrayal of Britain in twenty years time, the film is light years ahead of the ever popular but personally disappointing V for Vendetta, which stripped away British iconography and culture and essentially kept London as a rather two-dimensional metaphor for the United States.

As a thriller, the film is blisteringly intense and incredibly effective. From the bomb blast that caps off the opening credits to the frenzied urban warfare sequences that dominate the film's closing thirty minutes, Cauron never lets the film lag. Perhaps this is why Owen never seems rested and has a haggard look the whole time, maybe Cauron never stopped. Though it slows down enough to deal with character development and exposition, the film maintains a running intensity as Theo and Kee try to stay one step ahead of terrorists, the police, the army and random opportunists. Several action scenes are shot in continuous takes, and make for compelling and electrifying viewing.

However, the film works as a socio-political drama as well. Though Cauron's two central messages (that immigrants enrich, rather than threaten, Western society, and that the outlook for human survival is dim when operatives on all sides let ideology displace compassion and good judgment) are strongly put, he is never so heavy-handed that they dominate or displace the actual storyline. Similarly, while the film makes numerous metaphorical references to the political and military happenings of the early and mid 2000's events, they are never so contrived as to derail the narrative.

The film features solid performances from Clive Owen, who is at his rugged, rumpled best, and Julianne Moore. Supporting players also do well: Michael Caine is terrific as Theo's pot-growing hippie friend, the versatile Chiwitel Ejiofor is again in fine form as a revolutionary cell leader, and Pam Ferris is also good as another of Kee's protectors. It is, however, Claire-Hope Ashitey who stands out as the illegal immigrant who may well be humanity's hope for the future.

The episodic nature of the story makes Children of Men difficult to place into one genre alone. Briefly glimpsed futuristic sci-fi technology is grounded in reality and looks entirely achievable while grey, graffiti ridden concrete locations provide an excellent backdrop for the near satirical look of our current social and political climate. There's poignant drama interspersed amongst exhilarating action and yet enough twists to call it a thriller.

This is not to say it's flawless. Some exposition is handled better in places than others for instance. However Alfonso Cuarón has achieved a completely remarkable experience. Arguably the film could have been longer given how strong most of it is. The only really hard pill to swallow is the comedy juxtaposed with some stark imagery that looks all too familiar to anyone who has ever seen the News from the past few decades. Nice to see a Pink Floyd reference though (pigs might fly!), and someone finally found a use for Battersea Power Station.

I am surprised by level of misinformation about this event. I have shared some info at the place which shall not be named. Here is an explanation of what is going on and how it has started:

Greece Financial Crisis History:

  • Greece wanted to get into EU in order to borrow money at very low interest rates (one of the perks being in EU).
  • Greece applies for EU.
  • EU reviews their financials and say "Your financials are weak. Get your finances together and we will think about it."
  • Greece falsifies their financial documents to show their financials a lot better than it is.
  • EU accepts Greece into EU.
  • Greece starts borrowing money like crazy.
  • Loans are due to pay back. Greece cannot.
  • EU realized that they falsified documents and their financials are actually shit. They force them to make some changes such as cutting government spending and increasing taxes.
  • Greece obeys and makes the changes.
  • Due to lack of incoming capital into Greece economy, Greece economy sinks, unemployment sky rockets, riots starts.
  • Election time comes. Greeks elect a new president whom promised to stop obeying EU's orders. Thus promises to increase government spending and reduce taxes to help economy.
  • New president goes to EU with his plan. He asks for more loans to do that and he asks to delay re-payment of old loans.
  • EU says "NO". They only agree to give them more loan if they continue to reduce spending and further increase taxes, which new president do not want to do.
  • President calls for referendum, which means asking citizens of Greece what to do. The question is: Should we continue to obey EU's demands (increase taxes, cut government spending) to get more money from them, and stay in EU, or should we say screw you, default on the loan, leave EU, print our own money?

People of Greece has voted NO for the referendum which was conducted in July 5th 2015. There are many speculations of what this really means. Here are top two solid ones:

  • Prime Minister of Greece will take these results to EU and use it as leverage. In the end, if Greece leaves Eurozone or EU, that is a bad thing for EU and the value of Euro. Thus, Germany and other countries who landed money to Greece may be taken back by this result and they may go easy on the conditions of the new loan Greece is trying to get. The Prime Minister of Greece will play on this hard, basically he will tell EU that if they do not give money under better conditions, they will take following approach.
  • If Greece and EU cannot come to an agreement for the new loan, or if Greek government does not want any more loans, then Greece will leave Eurozone for sure and even possibly EU. Leaving Eurozone means Greece will be able to print their own money, and invest that into their own economy. Doing so, they will boost their economy hoping to bring more investors to the country, thus creating more jobs and more spending power. If they choose to do this, the value of the new currency will be really really low (good thing for tourists). Given economic conditions of surrounding countries, I am expecting the value of the new currency to be 1/4th of Euro. First couple of years will be really hard for Greek people, however, there is a good chance that the economy will pick up in the long run and Greece will be able to sustain their own economy with their own lifestyle.

Nevertheless, a piece of history is being written in our lifetime. This situation will be in economy books in the future years for sure. It is kind of exciting to see a piece of history unfolds as a country tries to shape itself to remove themselves foreign debt.

This is a short post, intended to outline some thoughts I've had. There might be more on this on my blog at some point in the future, if I can be bothered to dig up some more sources.

Multicellular organisms like plants and animals tend to harbor a variety of viruses, bacteria and parasites. There exists an evolutionary arms race between these organisms. The organisms develop new mutations that allow them to thrive in our bodies, which causes more of us to die, which causes us to genetically adapt to these diseases.

In the case of humans, an interesting example is the flu. Most of us don't die from the flu, because the flu has killed millions of people for countless generations. Thus we genetically adapted to the flu. On the other hand, Native Americans never had any exposure to the flu. Thus when they came in contact with the flu, millions of them died as a result.

Now, evolution depends on mutations, but every individual organism that's born carries some unique mutations. The more specimens of an organism exist, the more new unique mutations emerge. This leads to the fact that when more individuals of a species exist, more unique mutations are "tested" every generation. This causes evolution to accelerate.

In the case of humans, we have started to evolve much faster since the Neolithic revolution. The authors of the 10.000 year explosion seem to believe we may have evolved 100-times faster during the period after the Neolithic revolution than we did when we were still hunter-gatherers.

Of course, for diseases that infect us, the same principle applies. When they can produce more copies of themselves, they can evolve faster. A hundred humans infected with malaria means that malaria gets to try out about 100 times as many mutations, which means malaria evolves 100 times as fast.

This is probably also why we pursue an exterminationist campaign against pathogens. We want to remove any disease causing organism from the face of the planet, because it can now evolve very rapidly due to the sheer abundance of humans on our planet, as there are around 1000 times more humans today than there were 12.000 years ago.

Note that a whole bunch of illnesses seem to be jumping species, into the human population. The Middle East Coronavirus jumped from bats to camels to humans. The Ebola virus jumped from bats to humans. The HIV virus jumped from apes to humans. Longer ago, in the medieval era, the measles virus jumped from cows to humans. In fact, the majority of disease we suffer is believed to originate from other animals.

So, if this happens in humans, where else do you think it might happen? Well, our domesticated plants and our domesticated animals will face the same problem. The land area dominated by humans has increased drastically. In the year 500, just 0.8% of the land's surface was dominated by crops. By 2000, 10.6% of land was. These crops are now also grown more intensively, are less genetically diverse and belong increasingly to just four species (rice, wheat, soy and maize).

It is estimated that in 5000 BC, 0.048 million square km was used to grow our crops. In the year 2000, 15.32 million square km is used to grow our crops. In those 7000 years, we would estimate that there has been conservatively speaking about a 300-fold increase in the population of these species that we use for agriculture. Assuming that they are not kept artificially sterile with pesticides, we would expect to witness a 300-fold increase in the rate of new mutations in pathogens that infect these plants. For our pastures, the land used has increased from 0.004 million square km in 5000 BC, to 34.29 million square km by the year 2000. Thus we would expect to witness almost a 10.000-fold increase in the rate of new mutations in pathogens that infect these animals. In practice we find a situation where the farmers administer antibiotics to their animals, even though the animals may be healthy.

In nature, we often find a certain degree of hysteresis, that is, a delayed response to a change. Let's take an example of foxes and rabbits. If the rabbits increase their population, the foxes have more food. Thus the fox population begins to grow as well. However, there exists some time where the fox first has to eat rabbits, gain weight as a result, mate, become pregnant, give birth, etcetera. Thus, the peak in fox population, follows the peak in rabbit population, rather than peaking simultaneously with the rabbit population. What happens in fact is that the rabbit population drops below its carrying capacity, because the peak in foxes occurs after the peak in rabbits.

In our case, there exists hysteresis as well. The pathogens that infect our crops, our domesticated animals and our own bodies, have to evolve to feed off our excess biomass, a process that takes some time. As an example, it took the Ug99 wheat stem rust a few decades to emerge after we started planting stem-rust resistant wheat everywhere. Similarly, it can take quite a long time for a disease in one plant species to jump species to one of our crop species. It might for example take a decision on our part to start growing corn outside of America, before corn is exposed to a new disease that did not occur in pre-contact America.

Thus, the conclusion here is that when civilization collapses, diseases will continue to adapt to the plants and animals we have domesticated, as well as to our own bodies. In addition, the more land we dominate, the faster the ecosystem adopts to our presence and begins to push back against our presence. In this context, the human population presence in tropical lands is especially important, as this is where most biodiversity exists and thus the most potential exists for disease to jump species into our population.

Eventually, the ecosystem we inhabit forces our species back to a fraction of our current population, I would suspect somewhere in the range of a few million individuals at most. I hope that I will one day reincarnate and live to see the post-civilization world, where just a few million humans live as hunter-gatherers and plants grow over derelict skycrapers. If not, I trust that at least some of the atoms that now compose my body will at some point be incorporated into wild plants and animals and (post-)humans who will traverse the now depopulated landscape, as my body continually sheds dead skin cells and a variety of bodily fluids in various places around the world.
